message.content:
In lions, one of the most striking examples of a dominant genetic trait is the **presence of a mane in adult males**. The gene that controls mane development is expressed dominantly, meaning that a single copy of the allele is enough for a lion to grow a mane. This trait is strongly linked to testosterone levels and is typically seen only in mature males, while females and juveniles do not develop a mane even if they carry the allele.

Another classic example is the **tawny (golden) coat color**, which is also governed by a dominant allele. Lions with at least one copy of the dominant allele will display the typical golden fur, whereas the recessive allele can produce a darker or black‑tinged coat in rare cases.

These traits illustrate how dominant genes can shape key physical characteristics in lions.
